n3d58dcf86d04: Reference data are important for accurate estimation of population substructure, yet sufficiently large reference samples are often unavailable for some populations. This limitation is especially important for methods that estimate population substructure from genetic summary data using reference allele frequencies derived from reference samples, such as Summix2. Here, we systematically evaluated how reference sample size for five continental reference groups [African (AFR), East Asian (EAS), European (EUR), Indigenous American (IAM), and South Asian (SAS)] affects Summix2 substructure estimates in simulated Latino-like, African American-like, and Peruvian-like populations, as well as real African American genetic data. We show that small reference sample sizes introduce systematic bias in substructure proportion estimates. We identified a sample size threshold of 150 individuals per reference group for accurate estimates with a mean estimation error below 0.05. We also developed two bias corrections: a simple inverse sample size correction and a flexible power-law correction. The power-law correction provided the greatest reduction in mean estimation error when all reference groups had small reference sample sizes, whereas the simple inverse sample size correction performed better when a single reference group had a small reference sample size. These findings provide practical guidance and bias adjustments for reliable population substructure estimation from genetic summary data, particularly when reference populations have small sample sizes. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. nb9cc64bdf06b: Genome instability is a central hallmark of cancer and it is characterized largely from sequence: mutation, copy-number change and rearrangement scored against a linear reference. The genome has additional degrees of freedom, such as the physical form (topology) of the DNA itself. A specific mode of localized genome dynamics changes both dimensions (sequence and topology) at once: defined chromosomal regions are also represented as extrachromosomal circular DNA (eccDNA). The biogenesis of eccDNA is a feature of many cancers, supplying the tumor with genetic elements that can participate in phenotypic selection, and supplying the observer with a window into the genomic instability landscape. Genome-wide maps of where these circles arise have not been available at scale or at high resolution. Building such maps requires physical selection of circular species, because most sequenced reads from unselected DNA derive from unrearranged sequence, conflating the signal from dynamic rearrangements with that from bulk chromosomal DNA. Here we combine biophysical and biochemical isolation of circular DNA with next-generation sequencing, applying it to a panel of cancer cell lines and to patient tumors, with non-cancerous cells and adjacent normal tissues as controls. The resulting genome-wide maps of the circular-element repertoire, the Circulome, reveal a consistent and previously unreported enrichment of these elements at particular chromosome ends. The circles map to regions extending well past the telomeres, reaching varying distances up to tens of megabases inward. This activity is accompanied by corroborating rearrangements within the linear genome, consistent with regions of chromosomal instability. Together these features define a spatially localized mode of instability in cancer, which we term Erosion at Distal Genomic Ends (EDGE). We formulate a classification problem to discriminate bladder tumor from matched normal tissue, finding that the EDGE signal outperforms the mean of all interior chromosomal regions, for each chromosome. These findings define a distinct spatial signature of cancer chromosome instability detectable through Circulome analysis, and connect early models of region-specific instability to the human cancer genome.
n3d0f4d816888: We demonstrate that the enzymatic activity of alpha-amylase (AA) can serve as an effective physicochemical trigger for membrane remodeling in giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs). This work provides insight into how primitive protocellular reactions directly translate into the membrane's mechanical responses. Analysis of the potato starch utilized in this work is composed of ~26\% amylose and ~75\% amylopectin. Quantitative DNS analysis revealed time- and concentration-dependent accumulation of reducing sugars during starch degradation by AA. The HPLC-RID chromatograms demonstrated the synthesis of glucose, maltose, maltotriose, maltotetraose, maltopentaose, maltohexaose, and maltoheptaose, with maltose and maltotriose as the major products. The accumulation of these soluble hydrolysis products gradually increases the osmolarity of the extracellular medium surrounding the vesicles, leading to osmotic asymmetry across the membrane. This biochemical framework provides a quantitative basis for understanding membrane deformation, curvature generation, vesicle deflation, and budding. In addition to the specific starch--$\alpha$-amylase system studied here, our work uncovers a general mechanism by which external biochemical reactions control membrane shape transformations via osmotic coupling. Such enzyme-driven remodeling offers a simple yet powerful strategy for inducing dynamic structural changes in artificial cells. It may provide insight into primitive protocellular processes in which metabolic activity and membrane mechanics were inherently coupled. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. nd3df908a9c81: Living systems operate far from thermodynamic equilibrium, sustaining complexity through continuous free-energy influx and heat dissipation. Yet the higher-order functional constraints imposed by non-equilibrium dynamics remain largely unexplored. To formalize how changes in cellular entropy production constrain intracellular organization across proliferative state transitions, we developed a stochastic-thermodynamic model linking reduced dissipative drive to transient increases in intracellular configurational entropy. Within this framework, we examined abundance-weighted predicted RNA folding stability as a transcriptome-level projection of the intracellular configurational remodelling. Consistent with the model, transcriptome reorganization across the cell cycle produces coordinated, phase-dependent changes in the distribution of transcript-level RNA folding free energies. Extending this analysis to stress adaptation, we find that human cancer cells exposed to molecularly targeted agents and nutrient-limited Escherichia coli converge on expressed RNA pools enriched for transcripts with less negative RNA folding free energies, despite marked heterogeneity in the transcriptional responses within each system. Opposing shifts during acquired resistance under continued drug exposure and bacterial recovery from starvation further support an association with growth state. Together, these findings suggest that transcriptome organization extends beyond gene-regulatory programs to collective biophysical properties that may reflect non-equilibrium constraints shaping cellular-state transitions.
n6be3c5486fde: Inflammatory memory in barrier tissues often manifests as exaggerated recall responses to previously encountered stimuli. While recall is generally thought to reinforce the Type of inflammation (e.g., Type 1 (T1), Type 2 (T2), or Type 17 (T17)) induced in the primary encounter, whether and how memory responses engage programs beyond the initiating Type is unclear. Here, we adapted well-characterized murine models of T2 atopic dermatitis (AD)-like and T17 psoriasis-like inflammation into repeated challenge paradigms to compare how inflammatory memory is stored and recalled through longitudinal single-cell RNA-sequencing. In T17 inflammation, a network of IL-17-producing γδT cells, IL-17-responsive keratinocytes and myeloid cells established in primary challenge re-emerged in recall with increased abundance and accelerated kinetics. By contrast, allergic T2 memory drove a particularly exacerbated and durable recall response in which hallmark features of T1 immunity, including interferon (IFN) signaling and cytotoxic lymphocyte recruitment, were unexpectedly layered onto amplified T2 responses. This T2-to-T1 shift was initiated by CD8+ tissue-resident memory T (Trm) cells that expanded with repeated challenge, produced IFNγ, TNF-α and IL-13, and closely resembled treatment-refractory Trm cells in AD. Tissue rewiring was supported by Trm-derived T1 cytokines and the IL-4-rich T2 milieu whose synergy on fibroblasts amplified allergic recall via IL-15 and CCL19. By tuning fibroblast IFN responsiveness in vivo, we mechanistically dissect how this fibroblast-CD8+ T cell circuit supports cytotoxic CD8+ T cell responses. In human AD, both arms of allergic recall amplification by this two-cell circuit featuring T1 and T2 effector responses were conserved. Our findings reveal how a stromal-immune circuit drives a clinically relevant T1 immune axis to support allergic inflammatory memory. ### Competing Interest Statement J.O.M. reports compensation for consulting services with Tessel Biosciences and Radera Biotherapeutics. n6dd520a1b681: The evolutionary transition from free-living bacteria to host-adapted symbionts is typically accompanied by substantial genomic changes. Within the genus Serratia, this transition has so far been documented only in the aphid-associated species, Serratia symbiotica, whereas all other Serratia species are free-living. In this study, we identify a putatively new Serratia taxon using metagenomic approaches in the trombidiform mite, Halotydeus destructor. We provide genomic evidence for a possible transition to a host-adapted lifestyle in this new Serratia sp., which sits phylogenetically within a clade of free-living Serratia species. The genomic signatures of evolving toward a host-adapted lifestyle include a reduced genome size and coding capacity, an elevated transposase fraction, and detectable chromosomal rearrangements, relative to other free-living Serratia species. However, the species does not show the same structure of genome reduction as S. symbiotica. Functional gene content analyses including COG categories and virulence factor repertoires also showed that our new Serratia sp. had a distinct gene profile from both free-living Serratia and S. symbiotica. Additional genomic screening suggests that infections of the new Serratia sp. are common in wild populations of H. destructor across its invasive Australian range, warranting future investigations on the possible role this symbiont plays in the evolutionary ecology of its mite host. Our work not only highlights a potential parallel transition to a host-adapted lifestyle in the Serratia genus, but also represents the first characterisation of a possible host-adapted Serratia taxon in a trombidiform mite. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest.
n400c3bf236ea: cAMP (cyclic adenosine monophosphate) is a crucial intracellular messenger involved in neuromodulation and plasticity, but more information on its spatiotemporal regulation is desirable. Here we constructed a red fluorescent indicator based on a truncated cAMP binding site derived from a regulatory PKA subunit of protozoan origin. It contains a single binding site for cAMP highly specific for cAMP over cGMP. chILI (cAMP highly-responsive Intensity and Lifetime Indicator) can be imaged as an intensity-based probe, but alternatively also offers options for fluorescence lifetime imaging. When expressed in the mouse brain using AAV-vector mediated gene transfer, it reports spontaneous and evoked cAMP transients from CA1 neurons in the hippocampus of awake mice. chILI will add valuable options for monitoring cAMP in vitro and in vivo. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest.
n7fa23282f95e: We develop an All-atom Structure Tokenizer that compresses biomolecular geometry into discrete structural tokens and achieves high-accuracy all-atom reconstruction. A hierarchical geometric encoder and finite scalar quantization map chemical units to a shared vocabulary of 8,192 tokens, while a joint coordinate de-tokenizer reconstructs backbone, side-chain, nucleic-acid, and ligand heavy atoms. The tokenizer achieves all-atom lDDT scores of 0.832 and 0.835 on CASP14 and CASP15, respectively. Building on this tokenizer, we train AtomLM-9b, an autoregressive language model based on Qwen3.5-9B that predicts structural tokens from molecular identities and connectivity and decodes them into complete atomic structures. We demonstrate, for the first time, protein structure prediction performance comparable to AlphaFold 3 with an all-atom-tokenizer-based structural language model: on the FoldBench protein-protein task, AtomLM-9b achieves a success rate of 75.01%, compared with the published AlphaFold 3 result of 72.93%. These results establish discrete all-atom tokenization as an effective interface between high-fidelity atomic reconstruction and language-model-based structure prediction. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest.
ndf53318ce69b: The incorporation of cytosolic proteins into bacterial outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) has remained mechanistically unresolved, as these proteins are normally excluded from vesiculation sites by the inner membrane (IM) barrier. Here, we show that antibiotic-induced envelope perturbation compromises this spatial barrier, enabling an aberrant interaction between proteins that are ordinarily segregated across cellular compartments and thereby promoting MV formation in Salmonella. Exposure to non-lethal cephalexin (LEX) induced robust hypervesiculation, accompanied by inhibition of the essential division penicillin binding protein (PBP) 3 and accumulation of the PBP5. Under envelope perturbing conditions, PBP5 accumulated at lateral sites associated with MV emergence and promoted periplasmic crowding independently of its catalytic activity. A cytosolic acyl carrier protein (ACP) emerged as a PBP5 interacting partner under LEX exposure, coinciding with cryogenic electron microscopy detected IM perturbation and aberrant ACP mislocalization. Formation of the PBP5 ACP complex promoted PBP5 accumulation, resulting in periplasmic crowding, progressive weakening of outer membrane peptidoglycan tethering, and ultimately MV formation. Together, these findings uncover a mechanism whereby stress-induced disruption of subcellular compartmentalization enables a non-canonical interaction between normally segregated proteins, driving hypervesiculation in Salmonella.
n005c70bc0147: Determining where scientific foundation models generalize beyond their development data is essential for reliable use, but aggregate benchmarks obscure performance limits and rigorous audits are difficult to conduct routinely. Here, we introduce AutoSPECTRA, a coding-agent protocol for systematic generalizability auditing. To inform its design, we reviewed 38 studies across five biological domains and evaluated coding agents, which generated hypotheses and empirical analyses but applied inconsistent standards for judging evidence. We then structured AutoSPECTRA around measurable generalization axes, prespecified analyses, controlled comparisons and independent confirmation. Across four biological foundation models, audits linked performance to protein sequence composition and relatedness to pretraining data (ESMFold2), representation of perturbations in training (STATE), effective spatial resolution (CONCH), and residue-level genomic, evolutionary and structural context (AlphaMissense). Agents also evaluated alternative explanations and rejected unsupported hypotheses. AutoSPECTRA provides a systematic approach to discovering and testing the limits of scientific foundation models. ### Competing Interest Statement P.C.S. holds several patents related to diagnostic technologies and is a cofounder and equity holder in Delve Biosciences and Lyra Labs, a board member and equity holder in Polaris Genomics, and an equity holder of NextGenJane. P.C.S. was formerly a co-founder of Sherlock Biosciences and a board member of Danaher Corporation, until December 2024. ndbac7843c6e8: B-cell epitope prediction remains challenging due to the limited availability of experimentally characterized data and the incomplete understanding of antibody-antigen recognition. Here, we present CARTnet, a novel contact-aware deep learning framework that integrates multimodal features and template-derived epitope information. CARTnet demonstrated superior performance when compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods across most evaluation metrics on both the internal and external test datasets. In particular, CARTnet achieved an AUPRC of 0.243 on the internal test set, compared with 0.220 for DiscoTope-3, 0.140 for BepiPred-2, and 0.198 for BepiPred-3. This improvement was also observed on the external test set, where CARTnet achieved an AUPRC of 0.267, compared with 0.192, 0.111, and 0.215 for DiscoTope-3, BepiPred-2, and BepiPred-3, respectively, supporting its generalizability. CARTnet also supports template-guided prediction, in which limited prior epitope information can improve the identification of additional epitope residues; a single template residue increased the AUPRC of the template-based variant from 0.225 to 0.403 on the internal test set. Furthermore, we demonstrated that epitope information from closely related viruses can be transferred across the genus Alphavirus to improve epitope prediction accuracy. These results establish CARTnet as an accurate framework for both de novo and template-guided B-cell epitope prediction.
n3978dac88c5f: An increased incidence of childhood type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) has been widely documented, but its pathophysiological origins are poorly understood. The post-World War II expansion of the plastics industry in the United States and elsewhere coincides with a marked increase in T1DM incidence; however, no pathophysiological mechanism has been proposed that could justify such a temporal correlation. Here, we leverage recent advances in artificial intelligence and protein structure prediction and binding to show that molecular mimicry is a plausible pathophysiological mechanism for plastic fragments to induce onset of T1DM for individuals with certain HLA haplotypes. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest.
nab39329d396f: Cellular diversity arises from both genetic lineages and non-genetic regulation of cell states, and knowing which cell states are tied to lineages is central to understanding how clones shape disease. Single-cell multi-omics technologies measure mitochondrial DNA mutations together with gene expression or chromatin accessibility in the same cells, but clones are usually inferred from mutations alone, making such clones difficult to identify. We developed CloneVI, a deep generative model that infers clonal structure from a latent cell state derived from gene expression or chromatin accessibility. It estimates the clonal probability of each cell from this cell state, together with the allele frequency of each clone by reconstructing the observed mutation counts. In simulated data, CloneVI recovered the ground-truth clonal structure in both single-clone and mixed-clone cell populations. In clonal hematopoiesis single-cell RNA-seq data with enriched mitochondrial transcripts, the inferred clones were associated with specific mitochondrial DNA mutations, and some of them showed high expression of a T-cell receptor variable-region gene. In chronic lymphocytic leukemia mitochondrial single-cell ATAC-seq data, CloneVI separated populations with different heteroplasmy levels and identified increased PAX9 accessibility. In a multi-donor ovarian tumor cohort, CloneVI captured mutant-cell populations enriched in particular cell states, and a differential test weighted by the clonal probability revealed the transcription factor activity of the cell state in which the mutant cells concentrated. CloneVI thus identifies populations defined by mitochondrial DNA mutations and associated with cell states in single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data. CloneVI is available at https://github.com/TaichiHIBI/cloneVI.
nfd1d4aafee16: Background: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disorder characterised by chronic inflammation and immune dysregulation, and neutrophils play a key role in its progression. COVID-19 also involves neutrophil hyperactivation that contributes to severe immune responses. Emerging evidence links COVID-19 to increased incidence or exacerbation of RA, potentially through overlapping immune mechanisms. Objective: To compare neutrophil transcriptomic profiles in RA and COVID-19 and identify shared immune pathways and disease-specific features. Methods: Publicly available neutrophil RNA-seq count data from the Gene Expression Omnibus were analysed: RA versus healthy controls (GSE116899) and COVID-19 versus healthy controls (GSE212041). A second COVID-19 comparison (severe versus convalescent) was assembled from GSE272381 and GSE227116. Differential expression was analysed with DESeq2, pathway enrichment with fgsea (Hallmark gene sets) and topGO (Gene Ontology biological process and molecular function). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were compared between diseases by direction of change. Results: In RA neutrophils, 11,355 DEGs were identified, of which 90 had an absolute log2 fold change of at least 2 with p<0.05 (70 upregulated, 20 downregulated). Twenty-four Hallmark gene sets were positively enriched at adjusted p<0.05, led by interferon alpha and interferon gamma responses, and Gene Ontology analysis highlighted type I interferon, antiviral and double-stranded RNA terms. In COVID-19 neutrophils, 420 DEGs were identified (37 upregulated, 383 downregulated), and no Hallmark gene set reached adjusted p<0.05. Of the 90 RA DEGs, 46 changed in the same direction in COVID-19 without reaching significance, and 27 changed significantly in the opposite direction, including CAMK1G, SIGLEC1, OAS1 and OAS3. In the second COVID-19 comparison, several of these genes, including OAS1, OAS3 and SIGLEC1, changed in the same direction as in RA. Conclusions: RA neutrophils show a transcriptional programme enriched for interferon and antiviral-response pathways. Part of the RA signature is shared with COVID-19 neutrophils, while a subset of genes diverges, and this divergence depended on the COVID-19 comparison used. These findings are hypothesis-generating and provide candidate genes for experimental validation.
n603e78077d3e: Evaluation of lymph node (LN) metastasis is critical for cancer staging and treatment planning. Since radiologic hallmarks of metastatic LNs are shared across primary cancers, a computed tomography (CT)-based deep learning (DL) classifier developed from one anatomy may transfer to others. This study built a DenseNet-121 ensemble model using clinical-implication-applied preprocessing and evaluated its cross-anatomical generalizability to LNs from diverse primary cancers. A DenseNet-121 ensemble model combining fixed-size cropping (FSC) and adjustable square cropping (ASC) was trained from ImageNet initialization on an axillary lymph node (ALN) dataset (n = 1,128 from 523 breast cancer patients). The model utilized clinical-implication-applied perinodal cropping with bicubic filtering and standardized resizing. To test cross-anatomical generalizability, an external dataset of 256 CT images across four anatomical regions was evaluated: cervical, mediastinal, upper-abdominal, and lower-abdominal LNs. Perinodal free margins were systematically varied from 10% to 40% to optimize the balance between context preservation and surround interference. Bicubic filtering and standardized resizing yielded the highest internal performance on the original ALN dataset (FSC-ASC ensemble area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.958, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.920–0.987 at 40% margin). The model demonstrated site-dependent, above-chance generalizability across all external regions. Cervical LNs achieved the highest performance at a 40% margin (AUROC 0.939, 95% CI 0.875–0.989). Mediastinal LNs peaked at a 10% margin (AUROC 0.796, 95% CI 0.672–0.903), with wider margins degrading performance due to adjacent structural interference. Upper-abdominal and lower-abdominal LNs reached optimal performance at a 30% margin (AUROC 0.814 for upper; AUROC 0.917 for lower). A single ALN-trained DL model can accurately predict LN metastasis across cervical, mediastinal, and abdominal stations through site-specific perinodal margin tuning. These findings support the feasibility of cross-cancer knowledge transfer and the clinical utility of generalizable backbones for pan-cancer nodal assessment. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest.
n2b8edb7fd2c4: The isolation-by-distance (IBD) principle describes the tendency for genetic relatedness to decline with geographic distance. Although the existence IBD has long been documented in natural populations, recent analyses of spatially referenced genotype data have shown that the strength of this relationship can vary across a landscape due to geographic barriers, habitat compatibility, or other factors. Effective migration surfaces (EMS) have emerged as a popular exploratory tool for visualizing spatial patterns in IBD. However, fitting likelihood-based EMS models is often computationally demanding, requiring repeated large-scale matrix calculations. Here, we introduce Deep Recovery of Effective Migration Surfaces (dreems), a graph neural network for amortized inference of effective migration surfaces. dreems maps genetic covariance and sampling locations directly to an effective migration surface, while simultaneously providing predictive uncertainty estimates. Once trained, the network accommodates different graph sizes and sampling designs without needing to re-train. Across independent coalescent simulations that were not seen during training, dreems has roughly 10-30% lower estimation error compared to a state-of-the-art likelihood-based method, with the largest gains observed under sparse sampling designs that are commonly encountered in practice. Reanalysis of several published datasets recovers spatial patterns that are broadly consistent with earlier likelihood-based estimates, while reducing computation time by orders of magnitude. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. National Institute of General Medical Sciences, https://ror.org/04q48ey07, R35GM151145, R35GM137919
nf1292fb827a0: Genome mining typically begins with known genes or protein families, which can make systems defined primarily by genomic organization difficult to detect. We developed a DNA-first framework combining asymmetric-covariance natural-vector representations with generic positional recurrence, joining separately calibrated signals through genomic coordinates. In benchmarks of array-associated reverse transcriptase (ART) loci, the target-free mathematical arm localized seven of eight predeclared loci, including all seven with exact-array coordinates. Dual-arm signals occurred in none of three non-array RT controls and in one of five UG27 systems, indicating selectivity within these small control sets. A separate profile-guided search of 6.12 Gb identified five candidate array-associated RT-like systems. In an independent 54.38-Gb evaluation of this profile-guided arm, structural compatibility was 24/32 under a historical-rule mirror, 12/32 after novelty-only selection, and 0/17 for architecture-selected complete ORFs; the two 32-member panels shared six exact sequences. Together, these results suggest that mathematical features of raw DNA can complement protein-directed searches in nominating genomic architectures for experimental RNA-to-DNA studies.
nce30c71a970b: The protein α-synuclein (α-syn) plays a central role in several neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson's disease; however, its physiological function remains enigmatic. We provide direct evidence by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, microscale thermophoresis (MST), and biolayer interferometry (BLI) measurements that the α-synuclein C-terminus binds to the vesicular SNARE (soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor) protein synaptobrevin-2 (syb-2), also known as VAMP2 (vesicle-associated membrane protein). The observed dissociation constant (Kd) in the 10 - 50 micromolar range falls within the estimated concentration range of α-synuclein in neurons, while local concentrations may be substantially higher. NMR chemical shift perturbation (CSP) and paramagnetic relaxation enhancement (PRE) experiments mapped the binding site with residue-specific resolution to the α-synuclein C-terminus (V118 - E137) and to the synaptobrevin-2 SNARE motif/linker domain interface (region A82 - K87), and also affected the synaptobrevin-2 N-terminus (M1 - S2). NMR CSPs and PREs indicate a transient interaction in the fast exchange (μs-ms) regime. These transient weak binding interactions are characteristic of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and allow both proteins to engage in multiple binding interactions, thereby enabling α-synuclein to play a regulatory role upstream of or during neuronal exocytosis. While the exact physiological role of α-synuclein remains debated, the involvement of its pathological form in several neurodegenerative diseases (dubbed synucleinopathies) is well established. Our data suggest a direct link between proteins involved in neurodegeneration and neuronal exocytosis.
n365af904d897: Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression involves stage-dependent transcriptional changes that are often masked by dominant cellular and biological variation. Here, we present ADVISE (Alzheimer's Disease Variational Isolation of Signal Embeddings), an interpretable deep generative framework designed to disentangle Braak stage-associated transcriptional signals from background biological variation through separate latent representations. Using explainable AI, ADVISE prioritizes genes and pathways contributing to the disease-specific representation. Applying ADVISE to large-scale single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from the human prefrontal cortex, we identify shared and context-specific signatures of AD progression across global, sex-specific, and cell-type-specific analyses, revealing convergent molecular programs involving synaptic transmission, HSF1-associated proteostatic stress responses, and SLIT/ROBO axon guidance. Notably, ADVISE prioritizes ROBO2 as a progression-associated candidate in excitatory neurons. Experimental validation using CRISPR activation in hiPSC-derived excitatory neurons demonstrates that ROBO2 activation reduces the phosphorylated Tau-to-total Tau ratio. ADVISE thus reveals context-dependent molecular signatures of AD progression and bridges human single-cell discoveries with experimental validation of candidate regulators of AD pathology. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest.
nf066df0b1950: Biomolecular condensates form through weak, multivalent, non-covalent interactions, but the role of covalent crosslinks in shaping their assembly and material properties remains poorly understood. We previously showed that disulfide bonds between cysteines in designer phase-separating peptides (PSPs) act as redox-reversible crosslinks that lower the saturation concentration (Csat) and help maintain condensate fluidity. Here, we ask which sequence features govern this behavior. We built two peptide libraries: one varying the inter-cysteine spacer length (2-10 residues) and one varying cysteine density (0-33%). Inter-cysteine spacers tuned condensate properties only modestly. Longer inter-cysteine lengths raised Csat from 300 to 900 μM, showed greater fluidity (as assessed by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) recovery rate, and resisted loss of fluidity during maturation; all inter-cysteine length variants dissolved and reformed reversibly over three redox cycles. Cysteine density, in contrast, was the dominant control parameter. Increasing cysteine density lowered Csat about 60-fold (1.5 mM to 25 μM) and reduced the fluidity by an order of magnitude. Its effect on fluidity was non-monotonic: condensates with up to ~14% cysteine density stayed liquid-like for 10 days, whereas those with 21-33% cysteine density in the peptide showed slower coalescence. Condensates with the highest densities also resisted dissolution under reducing conditions and showed sharply reduced uptake of a protein cargo (eGFP; ~60% to ~9%) and a small molecule (TMR, ~70% to ~45%), consistent with smaller mesh size. Together, these results identify disulfide crosslink density as a key lever for programming condensate assembly, viscoelasticity, redox responsiveness, and porosity. The results offer key design principles both for understanding cysteine-rich disordered proteins in biomolecular condensates and for engineering redox-responsive biomaterials.
n00deb0b14693: Complex I is a large membrane protein that transduces redox energy into a proton motive force across a biological membrane, powering cellular respiration. Yet, despite significant experimental and computational efforts, its long-range proton translocation mechanism remains poorly understood. Here, we combine nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy and site-directed mutagenesis experiments with multiscale classical and hybrid quantum/classical (QM/MM) simulations to probe how conformational dynamics is linked to proton transfer reactions in the terminal antiporter module (Nqo12/NuoL/ND5) of Complex I. We show that protonation of a conserved proton-loading site (Lys329/His241Nqo12) in the terminal antiporter-like module gives rise to conformational changes that result in opening of the proton pathway. We further show that this protonation reaction is controlled by buried ion-pairs that modulate the barrier for proton translocation by intrinsic electric field effects. On a general level, our combined findings reveal how bioenergetic machines combine conformational dynamics with hydration transitions to establish efficient redox-driven proton pumps. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. ne19a5226c6e9: Protein language models (PLMs) are powerful predictors of protein interactions, but strong benchmark performance does not ensure reliable discoveries. We introduce PPI-Caliper, a model-agnostic framework that adapts conformal calibration to select interactions at user-specified false discovery rate (FDR) levels using held-out labels without retraining the predictor. Across five species, two PLM-based predictors, and two human training-data versions for each predictor, PPI-Caliper keeps empirical FDR at or below the target level under in-distribution calibration. Under distribution shift, transferred thresholds tend to become conservative when predictive performance improves, but can fail to control FDR when performance deteriorates. PPI-Caliper connects pre-trained interaction scores to explicit error targets and demonstrates why reliable biological discovery requires evaluating calibration alongside predictive accuracy.
nfd7707c1824a: Endometriosis is associated with impaired endometrial decidualization, yet conventional differential expres-sion analyses cannot readily distinguish delayed transcriptional activation from reduced response amplitude.These mechanisms may produce similar expression differences at individual time points while implying distinct biological interpretations. Establishing when they can be distinguished is therefore a computational identifiability problem.We implement an identifiability-aware analysis of temporal displacement and amplitude attenuation in longitudinal transcriptomic responses. The approach combines reference trajectories, constrained amplitude-only and amplitude-plus-delay models, analytical examples of observational equivalence, and simulation-based assessments of mechanism distinguishability. Held-out time-point evaluation and culture-level sensitivity analyses examine the stability of model-dependent conclusions.In GSE246591, a candidate-delay-dependent dynamic-range filter excluded 30.9 - 38.3% of initially dynamic features under a hypothetical 24-hour shift across four endometrial stromal cultures. A two-component diagnostic separating retained dynamic range from affine shape similarity revealed that small projection residuals can arise from either loss of observable dynamics or similarity of response shapes. These findings demonstrate why a single separation statistic may be insufficient for interpreting temporal identifiability.Complementary independent in vivo analyses provided biological context. In GSE51981, an endometrial progesterone-response-associated transcriptional score was reduced in endometriosis samples (phase-model estimate 0.155, 95% CI 0.222 to 0.088). GSE6364 showed a directionally consistent but statistically inconclusive difference (0.033, 95% CI 0.068 to 0.002). Neither observation independently establishes a temporal delay.Together, these results support selection-aware evaluation of temporal transcriptomic responses, distin-guishing structural ambiguity and loss of dynamic signal from evidence of a biological timing change.
nec3a2bf18ece: A precise analysis of shape instabilities in cell-sized membrane compartments requires thorough quantification of the shape dynamics of individual components over extended periods. Herein, we have used phase-contrast microscopy to image giant unilamellar membrane vesicles (GUVs), which are widely used as model systems for cellular structures. GUVs were prepared in the fluid lamellar phase of 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine with and without cholesterol dissolved within a potato starch solution. The morphological changes and budding dynamics of individual GUVs with different chemical compositions were quantified using a deep-learning based image analysis framework over extended time periods, by using phase-contrast micrographs as input data. This automated framework integrates contour-based detection of the mother vesicle with precise segmentation of daughter compartments, thereby enabling explicit identification and tracking of mother and daughter vesicles at high temporal resolution. These findings further facilitate the measurement of the temporal evolution of vesicle morphometrics including area, and local membrane curvature during budding, that can be used as an input to develop computational models aimed at elucidating curvature-driven membrane remodeling in complex soft materials.
n44714bdd1723: Many aquatic invaders are crossing biogeographic boundaries from saline to freshwater habitats. This transition often requires acclimation or evolution of physiological mechanisms to maintain internal ionic homeostasis. Populations of the copepod Eurytemora affinis complex have repeatedly invaded freshwater environments from saline habitats over the past century, providing an ideal model for investigating rapid adaptation to salinity change. Prior studies have found that ion transport-related genes form the largest functional categories of genes under selection and show evolutionary shifts in gene expression across saline to freshwater transitions in the E. affinis complex. In this study, focusing on the top targets of selection, we investigated evolutionary and acclimatory shifts in gene expression for 19 ion transport-related genes for populations of E. carolleeae (Atlantic clade of the E. affinis complex). Using a quantitative real-time PCR approach, we compared gene expression between ancestral saline and derived freshwater populations through a common garden reaction norm experiment and a laboratory natural selection experiment. We found that different ion transport-related gene paralogs within expanded gene families showed divergent patterns of expression in response to salinity change, consistent with specialization. For instance, Na+/K+-ATPase subunit α paralog 1 ( NKA-α-1 ) and Na+,K+,2Cl− cotransporter paralog 3 ( NKCC-3 ) exhibited the evolution of increased expression in the freshwater population across all conditions, relative to the saline population. In contrast, Na+/H+ antiporter paralog 7 ( NHA-7 ) and NHA-5 showed evolution of elevated expression in the saline population under low salinity relative to the freshwater population. Several genes also showed evolutionary differences in plasticity between saline and freshwater populations, such that saline populations retained phenotypic plasticity, whereas freshwater populations were comparatively canalized. In the laboratory natural selection experiment imposing salinity decline, evolutionary responses of the paralogs NKCC-3 , NHA-5 , and NHA-7 in the saline selection line largely recapitulated the evolutionary shifts observed in the natural populations. On the other hand, expression patterns of the ion transporters in the freshwater selection line showed little response during salinity increase, suggesting canalization. Together, these results reveal evolutionary and acclimatory divergence in gene expression among paralogs, suggesting the evolution of functional divergence among them. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. n97ebc3147ea6: Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is emerging as a tool for large-scale ligand screening and fragment-based drug discovery, generating extensive collections of reconstructions. At the same time, the systematic inspection of local density variations remains challenging, particularly when identifying weak or partially occupied features. Here, we present Astex-Faro, a statistical framework that defines an expected specimen state from a reference ensemble and identifies significant structural deviations in a target map through comparison against this reference. Furthermore, the method allows the enhancement of weak or poorly resolved features, enabling the recovery of signals that would otherwise be difficult to interpret. Fourier Shell Coherence (FSCoh) is introduced as a metric that quantifies consistency across reconstruction ensembles. We show that Astex-Faro reliably detects subtle structural features and improves their interpretability across datasets spanning a broad range of experimental challenges, from highly homogeneous specimens to membrane proteins, low-occupancy ligands and fragment-screening experiments. Together, these developments provide a practical framework for cryo-EM screening, increasing confidence in hit identification and reducing the risk of missed binding events.
n7b1bf3ba08c0: Background and Aims: Floral scent is a primary driver of pollinator attraction and reproductive isolation in deceptive orchids. Yet, little is known about the variation and evolution of scent in a phylogenetic framework and how pollination affects the biosynthesis and emission of scents in these lineages. This study characterizes scent diversity across Cypripedium, a genus of deceptive orchids, examines phylogenetic constraints, and investigates post-pollination effects on scent composition in one of the species. Methods: Floral volatile organic compounds (VOCs) were sampled from 31 Cypripedium taxa using dynamic headspace techniques, and analysed by gas chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry (GC/MS). Uni- and multivariate methods were used to analyse intra- and interspecific scent variation and test for phylogenetic signal in floral scent. Post-pollination effects on scent composition were experimentally tested in C. henryi using four pollination treatments, combined with RNA-seq analyses of floral tissues to examine transcriptional responses in VOC biosynthetic pathways. Key results: We detected 258 floral VOCs, revealing a high chemical diversity dominated by terpenoids, aliphatics, and aromatic compounds. Floral scent composition was highly species-specific, and closely related taxa often shared only few compounds. Scent composition differed among pollination groups, but these groups explained only a limited proportion of overall scent variation. We detected a significant but weak phylogenetic signal, suggesting limited evolutionary constraint in floral scent. Pollination had limited effect on C. henryis floral scent and volatile biosynthesis gene expression, despite a significant decrease in total scent emission after pollinium deposition. Transcriptional changes predominantly occurred in the petals rather than the labellum and staminode. Conclusion: Floral scent evolution in Cypripedium is characterized by high chemical diversity, and a weak phylogenetic constraint, consistent with variable selection in food-deceptive systems. The pollination study further suggests the absence of a strong, directed post-pollination effect on the floral scent of C. henryi. Keywords: Cypripedium; deceptive pollination; floral scent; volatile organic compounds (VOCs); phylogenetic signal; linalool; post-pollination effects; transcriptome profiles; differential gene expression; floral organs ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest.
n2c53778e540d: Protein biosensors are important analytical and diagnostic tools that convert molecular recognition into measurable activity. Most common two-component biosensors require two non-competing recognition domains, yet binding affinity and specificity alone do not reliably predict their compatibility with the rest of the biosensor. We report a modular platform that exploits monomeric streptavidin (mSA2) as a surrogate recognition domain, enabling rapid functional evaluation of candidate binders in the context of biosensor scaffold without requiring a second ligand-specific binding protein. We established a chromatography-free protocol for recovering functional mSA2-based biosensor components from Escherichia coli. Using biotinylated small molecules methotrexate and vitamin D3, as well as heart failure protein biomarkers galectin-3 and S100A7 we demonstrate ligand-dependent reporter biosensor activation. The developed platform provides a scalable approach for rapid binder evaluation and biosensor prototyping, streamlining biosensor development using binding domains generated by directed evolution or computational protein design. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. n8985c40085f3: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) is a significant public health threat, demonstrating high rates of antibiotic resistance and frequently causing hospital-acquired infections. Bacteriophages (phages) are a promising adjunctive therapy to reduce bacterial load and manage VREfm infections. Many bacteria encode anti-phage defense systems--groups of genes that can counteract phage infection--but these systems have not been characterized in VREfm. Here we explored the diversity of anti-phage defense systems within clinical VREfm isolate genomes and examined their impact on phage susceptibility. We first used two available bioinformatic tools (DefenseFinder and PADLOC) to identify putative anti-phage defense systems in 21 hybrid-assembled VREfm clinical isolate genomes, and observed that most anti-phage defense systems were located on plasmids, defense islands, and prophages. Combining this information with functional testing of phage susceptibility did not reveal robust associations between specific defense systems and resistance to four VREfm-targeting lytic phages. Due to inherent limitations of phage susceptibility testing, we next developed an assay to assess phage survival after co-incubation with bacteria, and identified over two dozen genes associated with phage killing, including a potentially novel defense island. Lastly, we attempted to functionally validate 10 candidate anti-phage defense systems, only four of which were ultimately tested in enterococci. Expression of one of these candidates, AbiE, decreased bacterial susceptibility to two Enterococcus-targeting phages. As VREfm-targeting phage therapy becomes more widely available, identification of genes contributing to phage resistance can aid in streamlining the provision of phages to patients who could benefit from this new therapeutic modality.
nc066572bf146: The two variants of GUTS (General Unified Threshold model of Survival), stochastic death and individual tolerance, disagree about no-effect concentrations under time-variable exposure, and no standard test separates them. Each variant fixes two independent choices, which form a 2x2 classification: whether the hazard accumulates while damage exceeds a threshold (cumulative) or is set by the highest damage reached (peak-based), and whether repair is proportional or saturating. Calibration fit cannot choose: each structure fits by adjusting its own damage recovery, the cumulative one faster in twelve of fourteen compounds. For two identical pulses separated by complete recovery, the cumulative hazard predicts equal survival through both whatever the parameters, so a carry-over ratio (second-to-first survival) above one excludes it; in Gammarus pulex fourteen of fifteen ratios are at or above one, seven significantly. The peak-based hazard predicts the ratio's maximum, approached as intervals lengthen in five of six compounds. For organophosphates, whose recovery outlasts the published pulse intervals, the one test on measured damage favours the peak-based hazard: diazinon-exposed Daphnia magna stopped being immobilised once acetylcholinesterase, still inhibited, began to recover. The peak-based hazard is the appropriate default for toxicokinetic-toxicodynamic risk assessment of narcotics and uncouplers, and provisionally of organophosphates.
nbc83f997d606: Long-read amplicon sequencing profiles communities at high resolution, but taxonomic accuracy depends on the reference, classifier and the parameters used. Here, we present HiFiTaxa, a reproducible, single command Nextflow pipeline for PacBio HiFi 16S rRNA gene and fungal ITS amplicons. It builds versioned references from current GTDB and UNITE releases and supports Bayesian lowest common ancestor (BLCA) and naive Bayes (NB) classifiers and the read level profilers Emu (16S rRNA gene) and EMITS (ITS). We benchmarked them on mock communities and on holdouts with 10% of GTDB or UNITE databases sequences withheld. On the 16S rRNA gene mock of 20 species, BLCA detected all 20 species and reported two false positives, NB detected 17 and reported none, and Emu detected all 20 and reported eight. In the GTDB holdout, for taxa represented in the reference, BLCA reached 80.0% species level accuracy against 48.1% for the exact matching species step of NB. However, NB produced fewer incorrect assignments for taxa absent from the reference. On fungal ITS, BLCA had slightly higher holdout accuracy at species level(54.7%) against 52.2% for NB. NB was more conservative for novel taxa, and EMITS detected the most mock species. HiFiTaxa therefore offers a single reproducible workflow that uses current GTDB and UNITE releases and enables users to choose between different classifier algorithms depending on their needs.
nd61269939d31: Coastal fish assemblages are influenced by environmental heterogeneity across horizontal and vertical dimensions, yet their fine-scale three-dimensional structure remains poorly understood. We investigated spatial variation in fish assemblages using environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding at 100 stations across three depth layers (300 samples) in Maizuru Bay, a semi-enclosed coastal bay in Japan. Concurrent hydrographic measurements were used to examine associations between fish assemblage composition and environmental conditions. We detected 216 fish species, with mean species richness decreasing from 28.4 at the surface to 16.4 at the bottom. Thirty-three species were detected exclusively below the surface. Fish assemblage composition differed significantly among depth layers and exhibited pronounced horizontal turnover along the bay axis. Although depth, geographic position, and measured environmental variables were associated with assemblage composition, they collectively explained only 13.0% of the variation. The independent contribution of spatial position (2.9%) exceeded those of depth (0.8%) and measured environmental variables (0.9%). These findings demonstrate substantial three-dimensional heterogeneity in coastal fish assemblages that cannot be fully explained by conventional hydrographic measurements. Our study highlights the importance of integrating horizontal and vertical sampling to characterize coastal fish biodiversity and improve marine ecosystem monitoring.
n93ba1b5bb02b: Background: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease driven by lipid accumulation and immune dysregulation. How chronic dietary lipid exposure reshapes T-cell states across vascular and lymphoid tissues, and whether these changes resolve after dietary normalization, remains incompletely defined. This study examined diet-associated T-cell remodeling and the contribution of macrophage-mediated stimulation. Methods: ApoE-deficient mice received a vegetarian diet (VD) or high-fat diet (HFD) for 12 or 24 weeks; a dietary reversal group received HFD for 12 weeks followed by VD for 12 weeks. CD45-positive cells from aorta, blood, spleen, lymph nodes, and bone marrow underwent single-cell RNA sequencing with matched T-cell receptor sequencing. T cell states were annotated using canonical markers, and exhaustion- and naive-associated programs were quantified using UCell scores. Analysis assessed T-cell composition, clonal expansion, and predicted macrophage-T cell communication, with splenic flow-cytometric validation. Results: HFD was associated with enrichment of exhaustion-associated states, with the highest exhaustion scores in the aorta. At 24 weeks, the pooled exhausted-cell proportion was 15.7% under HFD versus 10.6% under VD. Dietary reversal restored this proportion to 10.6%, while residual transcriptional changes persisted in a tissue-dependent manner. Flow cytometry corroborated increased inhibitory receptor expression and co-expression. Aortic macrophages exhibited inflammatory and antigen-presentation programs alongside increased predicted communication with T cells. Aortic T-cell activation and clonal expansion accompanied these changes, and clonotype size correlated with exhaustion score (Spearman correlation coefficient = 0.57, p = 0.029). Conclusion: Chronic HFD is associated with multicompartment T-cell remodeling, with prominent vascular exhaustion-associated programs and tissue-dependent recovery after dietary normalization. These findings suggest that dietary lipid exposure may leave a durable adaptive immune imprint across organs during atherosclerosis.
n320d96b12f74: Phenotypic heterogeneity within bacterial populations shapes adaptation, antibiotic tolerance, and infection dynamics, yet colony-level quantification remains difficult at scale and on dark/selective media. We present HeteroTyper, an automated, high-throughput time-lapse platform that measures colony phenotypes across >100 plates per run on both transparent and dark media. HeteroTyper includes a ready-to-use computational pipeline that can be deployed on common plate-imaging setups and across agar types, delivering appearance times as a proxy for lag times, growth trajectories, colony size, intensity, and morphology from routine image series. Automated counts closely matched manual counts, supporting accuracy and scalability. Using Yersinia pseudotuberculosis as a model, HeteroTyper resolves phenotypic heterogeneity in vitro, with early and late phases showing broader appearance time distributions than mid-log phases. It also reveals organ-specific heterogeneity in vivo, with mesenteric lymph node isolates displaying the broadest appearance time distributions compared to spleen and liver. Appearance time was negatively associated with final colony size and intensity, linking growth initiation to downstream colony outcomes. Together, these distribution-level measurements indicate that bacterial adaptation during infection is compartmentalized by tissue microenvironments and prior history, and establish HeteroTyper as a practical, generalizable route to quantify infection-relevant phenotypic diversity on solid media at routine, high throughput. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest.
naf2d230f1c4e: Eradicating toxic small molecules from the body typically requires the administrations of therapeutic agents for systemic circulation and tissue distribution, resulting in inevitable adverse events from off-target effects. Here, we propose a intestinal molecular siphoning approach for treating diseases caused by toxic substances, in which enzymatic degradation of a toxic substance in the intestinal lumen serves as a driving force for the diffusion of the toxic substance from blood to gut, and continuous elimination of the toxic substance in the gut could effectively ease substance dependence. Using nicotine as a model substance, a live bacterial system was constructed by displaying a trypsin-resistant nicotine oxidase on the surface of Bacillus subtilis spores, and encapsulating in enteric-coated microspheres for gastric protection and targeted intestinal release. After oral treatments with the live bacterial system in mice, peak concentrations of nicotine in blood and brain were remarkably reduced compared to controls. Moreover, the live bacterial system could effectively attenuate nicotine addiction by suppressing dopamine reward surges to reverse withdrawal hyperalgesia, preventing the upregulation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, and alleviating anxiety-like behaviors. These findings show the potential of intestinal molecular siphoning as a target-independent therapeutic strategy for lowering circulating toxic substances through non-systemic enzyme reprogramming.
n29c25eee73fd: Clathrin-coated vesicles (CCVs) mediate key endocytic trafficking events, and dysfunction of CCVs is linked to multiple human diseases. Conventional centrifugation-based purification protocols can enrich endogenous CCVs but fail to eliminate intraluminal smooth vesicles (SVs) and co-isolated exosomes; these lipid contaminants reduce sample homogeneity and hinder high-resolution structural and proteomic analysis. Here, we present an integrated workflow to isolate biologically active endogenous CCVs from porcine brain and reconstitute homogeneous, SV-free clathrin cages. Crude CCVs are first enriched by differential and sucrose density gradient centrifugation to deplete the majority of exosomes. Clathrin cages are then depolymerized under alkaline conditions, allowing separation of soluble clathrin and adaptor proteins from SVs and residual lipid contaminants via ultracentrifugation. Purified coat proteins are reassembled in vitro into uniform clathrin cages. Functional assays confirm that purified CCVs retain Auxilin-Hsc70-dependent uncoating activity, and the enclosed SVs carry active vATPase proton pumps. This approach produces well-defined samples suitable for cryo-electron microscopy and mass spectrometry-based investigation of clathrin assembly and disassembly. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. nf2d007b43f1d: Some genetic variants are associated with many traits, but a variant's GWAS statistics are also inflated by the effects of variants in LD with it and by confounding shared by all variants in a study. Existing measures of per-variant pleiotropy, such as counts of significant associations or multi-trait association tests, do not separate these sources. Stratified LD score regression separates them for one trait at a time and only through predefined annotations. We present LRCQ (LD score regression on {chi}2 across many GWAS), which estimates for each locus its phenome-wide heritability enrichment: the variance of its causal effects across a set of traits, relative to an average locus. LRCQ regresses squared Z-scores from 30 or more GWAS jointly on squared LD, with per-trait LDSC intercepts and heritabilities fitted in earlier stages. Its pooled least-squares solution has a closed form whose cost does not grow with the number of traits. Its standard errors account for sample overlap and genetic correlation between GWAS. Squared Z-scores identify enrichment at the resolution of LD clumps, not single SNPs, so LRCQ reports clump-level estimates ("omni-loci"). These estimates can be aggregated over any functional annotation or gene set chosen after the analysis. In simulations with real UK Biobank LD and 30 to 1,000 traits, LRCQ was unbiased for its clump-level estimand. When GWAS share samples its test statistics are strongly right-skewed: normal-reference p-values were up to 10-fold anti-conservative at P < 0.001, and skewness-corrected p-values from the exact third cumulant restored type-I error and FDR control. Model-based standard errors were calibrated once the enrichment estimates plugged into them kept the polygenic background. It ranked enriched loci better than mean {chi}2, LD-normalised {chi}2, multi-trait omnibus tests and significant-association counts in 13 of 16 scenarios. Its main vulnerability was a misspecified LDSC intercept. Applied to 444 Pan-UK Biobank European-ancestry GWAS, LRCQ found strongly non-uniform phenome-wide enrichment: the SD of true clump-mean enrichment was 8.3, against a genome mean of 1. It identified 70 omni-loci (99 LD clumps) at FDR 5%, including CRP, CETP, APOB, AKTIP, SMOX, the SHBG region, CASZ1 and HNF1A. These ranked only moderately with mean {chi}2 and poorly with counts of significant associations. Gene-level phenome-wide enrichment rose with loss-of-function constraint. Phenome-wide heritability was 3-5-fold enriched in coding, conserved, 5' UTR and promoter sequence, and depleted in repressed chromatin. LRCQ turns hundreds of biobank GWAS into an LD-corrected map of where phenome-wide genetic variance lies, and complements its companion method LRCP, which estimates genetic-effect correlations between loci.
nd75f326820ca: The extent to which core genomes reflect strictly vertical inheritance remains debated, particularly in ecologically diverse bacterial lineages. Here, we investigate the evolution of the core genome of Methylobacterium, a major leaf-associated bacterial genus, to assess how evolutionary signals vary across genes and whether they relate to functions involved in adaptation to life at the surface of plant leaves (the phyllosphere). Identifying 1,099 protein-coding core genes across 293 genomes, we combined gene tree comparisons, phylogenetic network reconstruction, nucleotide polymorphism patterns, and functional enrichment analyses. We found that most core genes show some deviation from the consensus phylogenetic tree. However, this discordance is not randomly distributed. Across all analytical approaches, genes showing the strongest deviations are consistently associated with functions linked to life in the phyllosphere, including anoxygenic photosynthesis, protection against UV and osmotic stress. These genes are often grouped into conserved clusters in the genome. In particular, a large cluster involved in anoxygenic photosynthesis, including bacteriochlorophyll and carotenoid biosynthesis, shows strong variation in its evolutionary history and organization across lineages, despite maintaining a conserved core structure. Similar patterns of phylogenetic incongruence and gene organization are observed across related Hyphomicrobiales inhabiting the phyllosphere, suggesting that these functions extend beyond Methylobacterium. Together, these results indicate that evolutionary heterogeneity within the core genome is concentrated in genes involved in key ecological functions. While alternative explanations cannot be excluded, these patterns are consistent with horizontal gene transfer contributing to the diversification of traits important for survival and adaptation in phyllosphere bacterial communities.
nf4559f503526: Oxford Nanopore Technology enables direct RNA sequencing without reverse transcription (RT) and cDNA sequencing without PCR amplification, allowing investigation of how RNA preparation protocols bias sequencing data. PCR amplification is known to introduce biases related to expression levels, transcript lengths, and GC content. However, biases introduced by RT have been described more recently and their quantification remains more elusive. Using seven cell line datasets from SG-NEx, we compared nanopore sequencing of direct RNA, direct cDNA, and PCR-amplified cDNA. We identified hundreds of differentially expressed genes and isoforms between protocols, indicating significant changes in observed expression. Differentially expressed isoforms displayed expected amplification biases, and further we observed decreased PCR counts associated with higher m6A methylation levels on native RNA. We also found differential transcript usage in hundreds of genes across cell lines, showing substantial changes in measured isoform proportions between protocols. Analysis of structural differences between isoforms that switch dominance revealed that while some events involve simple RNA fragmentation, most involve complex structural differences including novel junctions (e.g. exon skipping, intron retention). Compared to non-DTU genes, inserted introns (exitrons) were significantly more common after RT and amplification. Furthermore, visualisation of raw coverage data proved crucial for qualitative validation of experimental findings.
nb0a682d34ec8: Respiratory virus infections are the leading causes of morbidity and mortality of infants and the elderly worldwide. Currently it is not known how Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) vaccination of infants can cause enhancement of RSV disease, highlighting gaps in our understanding about how viruses like RSV interact with the immune system. Here we address this and show that ERK MAP kinase signaling from Toll-like Receptor-7 (TLR7) detection of RSV and influenza, but not human parainfluenza virus type 3 (HPIV3), infections in bronchial epithelial cells (BECs) drives replication of the viruses. Virus infection is detected by pattern recognition receptors like TLR7 that bind to single stranded RNA (ssRNA) viral replication intermediates in late endosomes. Here we report that TLR7 is expressed in BECs and detects RSV ssRNA, causing ERK MAP kinase signaling. RSV and influenza use this detection and signaling in BECs to drive its replication and infection, a mechanism that counters TLR7s role in antiviral defence. Experimental blockade of TLR7 binding or downstream signalling through ERK MAP kinase decreased RSV and influenza replication, but had no effect on HPIV3. RSV viral loads in mouse and human females were higher compared to males, consistent with higher sex-dependent expression of the TLR7 gene from two copies of the X chromosome in females. In a TLR7 gain of function mouse model there was a significant enhancement of RSV replication and RSV eosinophilic and Th2 disease markers like interleukin-5 (IL-5). In summary, TLR7 is expressed in human lung BECs in the lungs where it acts as a factor in RSV and influenza replication and disease pathogenesis. We propose that this is a major factor in determining the sex-disparity of viral disease.
n83e316bf33f8: Accurate and reproducible metagenomic analysis is essential for effective infectious disease surveillance. Targeted diagnostics such as culturing, antigen assays, and multiplex PCR panels identify only predefined organisms and can fail to identify atypical or novel infections. Shotgun metagenomics offers hypothesis-free detection, but adoption is limited by workflow complexity, dependence on mutable reference databases, and high computational cost. To combat these challenges, we introduce MicrobeRT, an integrated suite of genomic language models fine-tuned to classify metagenomic sequencing reads across three tasks: (i) species level taxonomic identification, (ii) antibiotic resistance gene detection, and (iii) pathogenicity assessment. The framework builds on three pre-trained genomic language models - Nucleotide Transformer (Dalla-Torre et al 2025), DNABERT (Ji et al 2021, Zhou et al 2024), and HyenaDNA (Nguyen et al 2024) - leveraging their large-scale genomic pre-training, adaptability to downstream tasks, and, in the case of HyenaDNA, ability to capture long-range sequence dependencies. The models are fine-tuned on large, curated datasets spanning microbial, viral, fungal, and human genomes, including more than 500,000 genomes and 250,000 antibiotic resistance gene sequences. To evaluate the performance of our fine-tuned genomic language models across classification tasks, we developed a benchmarking framework that compares MicrobeRT against state-of-the-art (SOTA) bioinformatics tools. Across both simulated and empirical datasets, the models achieve strong performance while reducing computational overhead. MicrobeRT is released as open-source software, enabling further fine-tuning and reproducible integration of alternative models and classifiers. We also demonstrate seamless, drop-in integration by incorporating our fine-tuned taxonomic classification models as an optional add-on within the open-source TaxTriage pipeline (Merritt et al 2026). MicrobeRT demonstrates the feasibility of three clinically relevant multi-label analyses, offering a practical path to scalable, reproducible metagenomic diagnostics and enabling broader deployment of AI/ML-enhanced infectious disease testing. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. n0977b4000368: Plant and metazoan genome assemblies are being deposited in the International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration (INSDC) archives at an accelerating rate, but the biological context needed to interpret them, such as ploidy, cultivar, and subgenome structure, is often missing from the record: these attributes are optional in most submission checklists and, when supplied, are entered as free text. We describe the gap in three layers. Ploidy varies within a species and cannot be inferred from taxonomy; chromosome-naming conventions differ between assemblies of the same crop; and that inconsistency is concentrated in species named by subgenome and is not associated with the size of the research community, which points to the lack of a shared convention. As a case study, we built a pipeline that recovers these attributes from the publications linked to an assembly. On a benchmark of 82 assemblies, its current version reported one wrong ploidy, and across 1,059 plant assemblies an earlier, less strict version found the ploidy in a publication for about half; for nearly a third, it found a publication but no statement of ploidy in it. Recovery from the literature can annotate assemblies already deposited but cannot stop new ones from arriving incomplete. We therefore propose that ploidy, cultivar, and subgenome structure be captured at submission as mandatory, controlled-vocabulary attributes, building on existing INSDC and Genomic Standards Consortium checklists. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. Google Summer of Code
nd184a36ad55e: Rice blast, caused by the hemibiotrophic fungus Magnaporthe oryzae, is one of the most destructive diseases affecting rice production worldwide. During infection, M. oryzae secretes effector proteins that suppress host immunity and facilitate colonization. Here, we characterized MoALE1, a predicted effector that is structurally similar to members of the heat-labile enterotoxin/cholera toxin family. Using a yeast secretion trap assay, we demonstrated that MoALE1 contains a functional signal peptide. A MoALE1-GFP fusion localized to the biotrophic interfacial complex, indicating that MoALE1 is a cytoplasmic effector. Expression analyses revealed that MoALE1 is expressed during biotrophy, from 16 to 48 h post-inoculation. Transient expression in Nicotiana benthamiana showed that MoALE1 suppresses BAX-mediated cell death, suggesting a role in host immune suppression. To investigate its contribution to pathogenicity, a{Delta} moale1 mutant was generated and evaluated in rice infection assays. Deletion of MoALE1 significantly reduced disease severity but did not affect fungal growth, stress tolerance, sporulation, appressorium development, host penetration, or early invasive growth. In contrast, infection by the {Delta}moale1 mutant resulted in enhanced host H2O2 accumulation and increased expression of ROS-associated defense genes. Together, these findings identify MoALE1 as a biotrophy-associated cytoplasmic effector that promotes rice blast pathogenicity by suppressing host immune responses and provide new insight into the function of ADP-ribosyltransferase (ART)-like effector candidates in M. oryzae .
n4378bba3f222: Cells maintain asymmetric electrochemical environments across selectively permeable plasma membranes. Ion channels on plasma membranes redistribute small ions, whereas large openings such as gasdermin pores allow both ions and proteins to cross the membrane, generating a multispecies transport regime. The transport of charged ions and proteins shapes electrochemical environments, leading to osmolarity changes, which in turn promotes water influx and cell swelling. Although biologists have observed the phenotypic progression from pore formation to cell swelling for decades, the molecular transport events underlying this progression remain elusive. To elucidate how pore formation drives downstream cellular effects, we establish quantitative multispecies transport frameworks to investigate gasdermin-perforated cells. We start by developing a reductionist model and benchmarking it against analytical Donnan predictions. We then explore three-dimensional geometries containing individual pores or pore clusters that form either simultaneously or sequentially. We reveal that ion-protein timescale separation generates non-canonical Donnan-like states, pore and cargo properties tune local transport, pore clustering modulates osmotic gradients, and sequential pore formation produces feedback-dependent dynamics. This work deepens our mechanistic understanding of cellular responses to membrane damage and informs the therapeutic design of pore-forming proteins with tunable cellular effects. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. nfab17acabe2d: Interpreting a biological network often rests on the relationship between its connectivity and the functional groups annotated on it, such as pathways, complexes, or enriched terms. For example, whether a group forms a cohesive module, how groups overlap, and which proteins connect them. These relationships are often hard to assess visually when groups are numerous or overlap, and most tools represent membership only by node color. NORMA 3.0 is a complete client-side rewrite of its predecessors, delineating and laying out groups with convex hulls, bubble sets, or fog clouds. Multi-group nodes are rendered as pies and directed, and parallel edges retain their evidence channels. Eighteen 2D and nine 3D layouts are scored by silhouette width, outline intrusion and overlap, and benchmarked for group separation and run time. The implementation also includes edge bundling, network importers for six databases, 21 topological measures, group-level and enrichment statistics, comparison of up to ten networks, export of high-resolution images, and an Application Programming Interface. Availability and implementation: NORMA 3.0 is freely available at https://normaviz.org. The source code is available at https://github.com/PavlopoulosLab/NORMA.
ne3069899470c: Although sensory input arrives in a largely continuous stream, recall is temporally compressed, discontinuous, and often structured as events. However, the temporal specificity of recall-related neural activity within events, and the separation and cortical organization of recalled features relative to perception, remain poorly characterized. We analyzed functional MRI data recorded during viewing and free recall of an episode of Sherlock. A data-driven alignment between viewing and recall data identified neural recapitulation of corresponding narrative events and revealed information that distinguished moments within events, particularly in the association cortex. Features ranging from low-level visual to semantic information predicted recall reinstatement. However, differences in predictive performance among feature levels became smaller during recall, and their organization along the cortical sensory-to-association gradient reversed relative to viewing. Thus, temporal specificity within events can be preserved despite substantial reorganization of feature representations across the cortex during recall.
n1be3d59c71f4: Classic nanofluidic devices harness geometric confinement to modulate single polymer conformation and control chain dynamics. While classic nanofluidic devices have given rise to a range of applications, they are fundamentally limited by the static nature of their construction, which restricts real time control over molecular conformations. The reversible electrokinetic confinement (RECON) technique enables time-dependent control of DNA conformations in nanowells via dynamic modulation of field-induced confinement. Here, we demonstrate that applying dynamically varying confinement using stochastic and periodic signals can drive the confined polymer to access a range of non-equilibrium states, with the distinct configurations quantified via their radius of gyration tensor. For periodic driving, the device allows controlled cycling across conformational states, with distinct hysteresis observed in the shape anisotropy modulation. We quantify the interplay between the driving frequency, driving amplitude, and resulting hysteresis. Overall, our results establish RECON as a platform for active manipulation of single molecules, opening new avenues for studying non-equilibrium polymer physics and developing high-throughput, dynamically tunable nanofluidic devices. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. Fonds de Recherche du Québec  Nature et Technologies, https://ror.org/00b9f9778, 320394
nd7f9f9e2b53b: Protein language models (pLMs) learn rich sequence semantics from vast volume of protein sequences, yet the information encoded in their high-dimensional embeddings remains largely a black box, posing an interpretability challenge. Here we show that semantic features learned by pLMs can be decoded to reveal biologically meaningful signals using coevolutionary analysis without downstream supervised-training. Building on this insight, we developed MaskNGly, a zero-shot framework that identifies protein N-glycosylation sites directly from PLM-embeddings while achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art supervised predictors. MaskNGly is computationally efficient and intrinsically transferable, enabling omics-scale characterization of protein glycosylation landscape.
